mappings.note: That the account ties the journey to lived feeling -- a defining feature of the yatra-vrittant form, C-1.1-LO-15.
Why he pushed past Sand Hill to a further dune: to get the sunset unobstructed. The sunset-scene outcome C-1.1-LO-18.
What he reports of Kanyakumari's local people -- the local-life-and-unemployment outcome C-1.1-LO-17.
What 'prayatna ki saarthakta' means -- the climb rewarded by the sunset, C-1.1-LO-18.
Which sights were wholly new to the writer -- the first-hand novelty a travelogue turns on, C-1.1-LO-15.
Discuss the suggestions with classmates who have special needs and hear their view -- reasoned discussion of a social issue, C-2.1.
Watch a sunrise and a sunset and write your experience comparing them -- descriptive composition, C-2.2, rather than the argued opinion of C-2.1.
Write a travel memoir of a place you have visited using the form's elements -- creative composition, C-2.2.
Hold a class discussion on 'travel enriches us' -- reasoned oral expression, C-2.1.
Which qualities are needed to meet sudden hazards on a journey, discussed with classmates -- reasoned expression, C-2.1.

Mark India's other coastal states on a map. A geography exercise that no competency here states; it serves sensitivity to India's regional diversity, so the goal CG-4 is cited rather than forcing a literature or expression outcome.
Tabulate places you want to visit with state, terrain, climate and best season. Like the map task, an India-survey activity no competency covers, so the goal CG-4.
Describe Kanyakumari's setting, sights and jan-jeevan and contrast it with your own place -- local life, C-1.1-LO-17.
How digital buying and e-commerce help cottage industry -- a reasoned view on a livelihood issue, C-2.1. Not C-1.1-LO-17, which is the unemployment the TEXT depicts.
Gather and discuss government efforts to promote handicrafts -- a social and economic issue argued in class, C-2.1.
What difficulties classmates with special needs would face travelling -- reasoned view on a social issue, C-2.1.
Suggest what would ease their travel, given their particular needs -- C-2.1.
Test your suggestions with the school's special educator and refine them -- reasoned discussion, C-2.1.
Pick two passages showing the writer's resolve and refusal to give up. Selecting evidence for a trait is analysis, C-3.1; no LO here covers the writer's own character.
Study the listed elements of the form, then explain one of your own journeys through them -- LO-15 for the genre features, C-2.2 for the writing it asks for.
Read Nirmal Verma's 'Prayag: 1976' beside this text -- a second travelogue set against the first, C-1.1-LO-15.
Research Vivekananda's life and work and discuss it in class: LO-16 because the Vivekananda Rock is what prompts it, C-2.1 for the class discussion.
What he saw to the right behind the dune -- part of the sunset tableau, C-1.1-LO-18.
Fill in: the sun's disc 'chhoo gaya' the water's surface -- the verb choice in the sunset picture, C-1.1-LO-18.
The colours over the water after gold -- blood-red, then purple, then black. The sunset description, C-1.1-LO-18.
Assertion-reason on the scene going black and the coconut clumps seeming to beat their heads -- the sunset passage, C-1.1-LO-18.
Which way back he took in the dark. Content recall from the narrative, C-1.1-LO-14 (summarising the vishayvastu).
Which sand colours he had seen on the shore. Content recall, C-1.1-LO-14.
Fill in: he wished to 'rakh loon' a little of every colour of sand. Content recall, C-1.1-LO-14.
A wave wet his feet and he sensed danger. Content recall, C-1.1-LO-14.
What he did as the danger grew -- took off his shoes and ran. Content recall, C-1.1-LO-14.
Assertion-reason on colliding with the high rock while running from the waves. Content recall, C-1.1-LO-14.
Why people gathered at the ghat at sunrise -- to offer arghya. A living religious custom, so the cultural-values competency C-4.2 rather than the sunset outcome.
Statements setting the sunrise beside girls hawking shells and bearers serving coffee to official guests -- the local-life juxtaposition, C-1.1-LO-17.
What the graduate youth said of the rock -- 'at least it gives us this much inspiration'. The Vivekananda Rock and the feelings it stirs, C-1.1-LO-16.
What was happening at the temple while he stood on the rock -- part of the rock episode, C-1.1-LO-16.
Sails and the wings of kadal-kaks glinting alike between boat and shore -- a visual image, the bimb competency C-1.2.
Which trait the piece best shows: nature felt inwardly plus alertness to social reality -- the twin strands that define this travelogue, C-1.1-LO-15.
Why he was going over the bus timetable -- he was planning the onward journey. Content recall, C-1.1-LO-14.
Which description of the language fits -- easy, flowing and pictorial. Style analysis, C-1.2.
What lay on the far side of the rock, making him feel mocked -- an open shore with people strolling. Content recall, C-1.1-LO-14.
What he saw at night from the Cape Hotel lawn. Content recall, C-1.1-LO-14; item 64 asks about the STYLE of the same passage and is mapped to C-1.2.
How far out the Vivekananda Rock stands -- the rock outcome C-1.1-LO-16.
How many others were on the rock -- part of the rock episode, C-1.1-LO-16.
What the boat out to the rock was made of -- three rubber-tree trunks lashed together. The crossing to the rock, C-1.1-LO-16.
How he hid his fear in the boat -- by suspending his own awareness. The rock crossing and its inner effect, C-1.1-LO-16.
Fill in: four or five hundred educated young men out of work in a town of eight thousand -- the unemployment outcome C-1.1-LO-17.
What the jobless youths mainly do -- file applications and argue. C-1.1-LO-17.
What the graduate youth himself sold -- photo albums. Local livelihood, C-1.1-LO-17.
He cracked a shell and ate the flesh to show the writer -- how they live, C-1.1-LO-17.
Who said 'we eat shellfish and argue philosophy', and in what connection -- the line that carries the unemployment message, C-1.1-LO-17.
Analyse 'for a while I forgot that I am I' -- the state the rock and the sea put him in, C-1.1-LO-16.
The colours and feelings used in the sunset description -- C-1.1-LO-18.
Why he went on alone from Sand Hill to the higher dune and why it matters -- the pursuit of the sunset, C-1.1-LO-18.
How he hid his fear in the naavda crossing to the rock -- C-1.1-LO-16.
How he describes the sunrise and the social conditions in one breath -- the local-life-and-message outcome C-1.1-LO-17.
What his pull towards the nameless colours of the sand reveals about him. Evaluating the writer from a detail -- analysis, C-3.1, since no LO here treats his own character.
Why the bus timetable runs in his head at the close and what it conveys. This asks for the significance, not the fact, so C-3.1; the plain-recall version of the same detail is mapped to C-1.1-LO-14.

The effect of the simile of the sun sinking helplessly into a lava of water -- an alankar/bimb question, C-1.2. C-1.1-LO-18 is the nearest sibling but is specifically about adverbs animating the scene.
Why it is called a journey of self-discovery and not mere place-painting -- the nature of the form, C-1.1-LO-15.
Analyse the piece against the elements of the travelogue form -- C-1.1-LO-15.
What picture of Kanyakumari's social reality emerges from the graduate youth -- C-1.1-LO-17.
The outward journey carries an inward one -- the defining claim about this travelogue, C-1.1-LO-15.
The style of the night-lawn description -- C-1.2, style and imagery.
The features of the nature writing and how nature is experienced -- style and imagery, C-1.2.
The chief features of the language and style, with examples -- C-1.2.
Describe the passages of courage, danger and will to live. Assembling and weighing evidence about the writer -- C-3.1.
Nature's grandeur set beside the discords of human life: C-1.1-LO-17 for the social half, C-1.2 for the nature-imagery half.
Who wrote 'Aakhiri Chattan Tak' -- the author-introduction outcome C-1.1-LO-14.
Mohan Rakesh's birth city -- author introduction, C-1.1-LO-14.
Which play won him the Sangeet Natak Akademi award -- author introduction, C-1.1-LO-14.
Which magazine he edited -- author introduction, C-1.1-LO-14.
At what age he died -- author introduction, C-1.1-LO-14.
Which form the work belongs to (yatra-vrittant) -- genre identification, C-1.1-LO-15, not the author-introduction LO.
What land he calls Kanyakumari -- of golden sunrises and sunsets. The sunset material, C-1.1-LO-18.
Which side of the bath tank he stood on. Content recall, C-1.1-LO-14.
The three seas meeting at the rock where Vivekananda meditated -- C-1.1-LO-16.
What he felt with his whole being -- 'the expanse of power, the power of expanse'. The feeling the rock and sea stirred, C-1.1-LO-16.
What he briefly forgot taking in the horizon on three sides -- that he was a living man and a traveller. C-1.1-LO-16.
